stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In a corrosion study, engineers coated twelve steel strips with an experimental zinc-based film and left them outdoors for a full year. At the end of the year, the ______ were weighed to measure how much metal had been lost to rust.
explanation: Ask whether the blank noun owns the next word. The next word is the verb "were," and a verb can't be owned, so the noun gets no apostrophe. There are twelve strips, and "were" is plural, so you need the plain plural "strips." This is the first check in every SAT apostrophe question: the noun right before a verb never takes an apostrophe. Once that check is automatic, the two-noun versions take one step instead of four.

A.why: You put in an apostrophe because the word ends in s. Nothing follows "strip's" for it to own, though. The next word is the verb "were," so the apostrophe sits where it makes no grammatical sense.

C.why: You saw that there were several strips and reached for s'. That form only makes sense if the strips own the next noun. Here the next word is the verb "were," so the strips own nothing and you need the plain plural.

D.why: You left out the apostrophe correctly but lost the plural. "The strip were weighed" pairs a singular subject with a plural verb, and the passage says there were twelve strips.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: A sports scientist filmed one long jumper during twenty practice attempts to study how takeoff angle affects distance. Frame-by-frame analysis showed that the ______ takeoff angle varied by only two degrees across all twenty jumps, even though the distances changed considerably.
explanation: Ask whether the blank noun owns the next word. It does, because the takeoff angle belongs to the jumper, so you need an apostrophe. Then count the owners. The passage says the scientist filmed one long jumper, so there is one owner and you need 's: "jumper's." On the real test, the context sentence decides the owner count in exactly this way. You find the count first and then choose the form.

A.why: You saw that ownership was needed but chose the form for several owners. The passage says the scientist filmed one long jumper, so s' gives the wrong owner count.

B.why: You left out the apostrophe even though the jumper owns the takeoff angle. With no possessive mark, "the jumper takeoff angle" doesn't show who the angle belongs to.

D.why: You made the noun plural instead of possessive. "Jumpers" only counts jumpers and doesn't show ownership, and the passage mentions just one jumper anyway.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: To improve storm forecasts, a weather service compared readings from four rooftop sensors placed around a single city block. Although the sensors stood only a few hundred meters apart, the ______ wind-speed measurements during one thunderstorm differed by as much as 30 percent.
explanation: Ask whether the blank noun owns the next word. It does, because the wind-speed measurements belong to the sensors, so you need an apostrophe. Then count the owners. The passage names four sensors, and the plural already ends in s, so you add only an apostrophe after it: "sensors'." In this subtype, s' is the form students doubt most. If the plural ends in s, the apostrophe goes after the s and nothing else is added.

A.why: You saw that ownership was needed but gave the measurements to a single sensor. The passage names four sensors and says their readings differed, so 's gives the wrong owner count.

B.why: You got the number right but left out the apostrophe. "Sensors" is a plain plural and doesn't show that the measurements belong to the sensors.

C.why: You marked ownership twice. A plural that already ends in s takes only an apostrophe, so the extra 's after "sensors" is not standard.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Hydrologists monitoring a mountain watershed installed gauges on five small streams that feed a reservoir. During the spring melt, the ______ were rising at noticeably different rates, depending on how much snow still covered the slopes above each one.
explanation: Ask whether the blank noun owns the next word. The next word is the verb "were," and a verb can't be owned, so the noun gets no apostrophe. There are five streams, and "were" is plural, so you need the plain plural "streams." On the real test, the noun just before the verb is a common place for a decoy apostrophe. Checking what comes next rules it out.

B.why: You added 's even though the stream owns nothing. The next word is the verb "were," so an apostrophe there makes no grammatical sense.

C.why: You left out the apostrophe correctly but lost the plural. "The stream were rising" pairs a singular subject with a plural verb, and the passage says there are five streams.

D.why: You saw that there are several streams and reached for s'. That form only makes sense if the streams own the next noun. Here the next word is the verb "were," so the streams own nothing.
